subject: Polity
topic: President of India — powers II — mixed tiers
description: Veto powers, ordinance, emergency, pardon, money-bill, executive vs ceremonial roles

questions.stem: Which type of veto powers does the President of India NOT have?

options.option_text: Absolute veto — refusing assent to any bill
Pocket veto — taking no action indefinitely
Suspensive veto — sending bill back to Parliament
Item veto — striking down specific clauses only

questions.explanation: President's veto types in India: (1) ABSOLUTE — withhold assent (private bills, certain other bills); (2) SUSPENSIVE — return for reconsideration (NOT for money bills); if Parliament passes again, President MUST give assent; (3) POCKET — take no action; the Constitution doesn't fix a time limit. India does NOT have an ITEM VETO (clause-by-clause) — that's a US-state-governor power, not Indian President. Pocket veto famously used by President Zail Singh on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.

questions.stem: ORDINANCE-making power of the President is exercised under which Article?

options.option_text: Article 72, dealing with pardon and clemency powers
Article 123, when Parliament is not in session
Article 356, related to state-level emergency provisions
Article 368, dealing with constitutional amendments

questions.explanation: Article 123 — President's ordinance-making power. Used when both Houses are not in session and immediate action needed. Ordinance has same force as a law of Parliament. Must be laid before both Houses when they reconvene; lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved by both Houses. Cannot violate FRs / basic structure (justiciable). Re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution by SC (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017). Article 213 — analogous power for Governors at state level. Distractor 1 = pardon (Article 72). Distractor 3 = President's Rule. Distractor 4 = constitutional amendment procedure.

questions.stem: The President's PARDON / CLEMENCY power under Article 72 includes:

options.option_text: Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation
Pardon only, with no other clemency variant
Reprieve and respite only, in capital cases
Power to acquit during the trial proceedings

questions.explanation: Article 72 — President's pardoning power. Five forms: (1) PARDON — completely absolves the convict (record + sentence); (2) COMMUTATION — substitutes lighter sentence (e.g., death → life); (3) REMISSION — reduces sentence duration without changing nature; (4) RESPITE — lighter sentence due to special circumstances (pregnancy, age); (5) REPRIEVE — temporary stay of execution. Article 161 — Governor's similar power at state level (NO power over death sentence; that's exclusively the President's). President EXERCISES on cabinet's advice (Maru Ram, 1981). Mercy petitions famously delayed (Ajmal Kasab, Afzal Guru cases).

questions.stem: Three types of EMERGENCY are provided in the Constitution. Which is the MOST commonly invoked?

options.option_text: National emergency under Article 352 of the Constitution
President's Rule (state emergency) under Article 356
Financial emergency under Article 360 of the Constitution
Federal emergency, requiring full Parliament approval

questions.explanation: Three constitutional emergencies: (1) NATIONAL EMERGENCY (Art 352) — invoked 3 times: 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war), 1975-77 (internal — Indira Gandhi's controversial Emergency). (2) PRESIDENT'S RULE / State emergency (Art 356) — invoked over 130 TIMES (most common). Triggered when state's constitutional machinery fails; central govt takes over state administration. SC's Bommai judgment (1994) restricted misuse — SR Bommai vs Union. (3) FINANCIAL EMERGENCY (Art 360) — NEVER invoked. Distractor 4 — invented term.

questions.stem: On a MONEY BILL, the President can:

options.option_text: Either give assent or withhold assent — no return for reconsideration
Assent, return for reconsideration, or use pocket veto freely
Send back with detailed amendments suggested by him
Refer it to the Supreme Court for advisory opinion

questions.explanation: Money Bill (Article 110) — President can ASSENT or WITHHOLD ASSENT. Cannot RETURN for reconsideration (suspensive veto NOT available for Money Bills). Reasoning: Money Bills are introduced only on the President's own recommendation; sending it back for reconsideration would be circular. Distractor 2 — wrong, suspensive veto excluded. Distractor 3 — President doesn't directly amend bills. Distractor 4 — Article 143 Presidential reference is for advice on questions of law / constitutional importance, not for routine bills.

questions.stem: The President of India is CONSTITUTIONALLY BOUND to act on the advice of:

options.option_text: Only the Prime Minister, in all routine matters
The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
The Cabinet Secretary as the senior bureaucrat
Only the Speaker of the Lok Sabha alone

questions.explanation: Article 74(1) — there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to AID AND ADVISE the President, who SHALL act in accordance with such advice. (Originally said 'shall'; 42nd Amendment 1976 made 'shall' explicit; 44th Amendment 1978 added that the President MAY require the Council to reconsider their advice ONCE, but must accept the second advice.) President is thus a CEREMONIAL HEAD; effective executive power lies with the PM + Cabinet. Article 75 — PM appointed by President; other ministers appointed on PM's advice. Distractor 1 — PM alone isn't the constitutional advisor; the Council is. Distractor 3 — bureaucratic, not constitutional. Distractor 4 — Speaker has no advisory role to President.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the SUPREME COMMANDER of the Indian Armed Forces?

options.option_text: The Prime Minister, the head of government
The President of India, by Article 53(2)
The Defence Minister, in the Union Cabinet
The Chief of Defence Staff, recently created post

questions.explanation: Article 53(2) — 'the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President'. Largely ceremonial; operational command flows through the Defence Minister + Service Chiefs + (since 2020) the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS). The Indian Armed Forces salute the President. President-as-supreme-commander tradition mirrors UK's monarch role. Distractor 1 = effective head of executive but not formal supreme commander. Distractor 3 = political-administrative head of MoD. Distractor 4 — CDS leads the Department of Military Affairs but is subordinate to the President in supreme-command terms.
